analysis.one_liner: Designates 1.56 million acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness, barring oil drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill has 22 Senate cosponsors but has sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee since April 29, 2025, with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give permanent wilderness protection to roughly 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain in Alaska. Land with the wilderness designation cannot have roads, permanent development, or motorized and mechanical work done on it, which would shut off the coastal plain to oil and gas drilling. The bill was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where nothing has happened since.
analysis.who_benefits: Members of the public who value keeping the Arctic Refuge coastal plain undeveloped, and Alaska Native communities whose traditional way of life there depends on an undisturbed landscape, gain permanent protection. Future generations keep the option of an unspoiled Arctic wilderness rather than having the area leased out for drilling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and Alaska Native communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds about 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to the National Wilderness Preservation System, as shown on a 2015 federal map.
Wilderness status is permanent: it cannot be undone by a future administration, so the protection does not depend on which party holds the White House.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose the chance to drill in one of the largest untapped oil areas under federal land, and Alaska's state and local governments lose the royalties and jobs that drilling supporters say would come with it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies and Alaska's petroleum interests

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation would permanently lock the coastal plain against oil development, even if future energy shortages or changing conditions lead the country to want access to the oil believed to be there.

Alaska's state government relies on resource development revenue and has long pushed to open the coastal plain to drilling; the bill would take that potential revenue and the associated jobs off the table for good.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who weigh undisturbed wilderness, subsistence ways of life, and protection of a one-of-a-kind public resource heavily, the trade is clearly worth it. Those who weigh domestic energy production and Alaska's development economy heavily see the same permanence as the bill's biggest flaw: wilderness status forecloses drilling in a place believed to hold billions of barrels, with no flexibility to revisit the choice. The designation is permanent by design, so the cost side is real, not a technicality.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2025, and no further action has been taken on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Arctic Refuge Protection Act of 2025 in the Senate on April 29, 2025, with 20 original cosponsors listed on the bill.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day, and the public action record shows nothing after that referral.
Twenty-two senators are listed as cosponsors: 21 Democrats and 1 Independent, and no Republicans.

The bill would designate approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, a designation that bars roads, permanent structures, motorized vehicle use, and commercial development such as oil drilling on the land.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests and Alaska officials who want the coastal plain open to drilling are better off so far, because a bill with 22 Senate cosponsors has received no committee action and no vote while the Senate majority rests with a party that has generally favored opening the refuge to drilling.

for.name: Sen. Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 20 original cosponsors.

for.name: 21 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a Democratic-sponsored effort with no Republican support.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on April 29, 2025.

against.name: Alaska's U.S. Senators
against.what_they_did: Have long and publicly supported opening the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling and opposed wilderness designation for it, and neither cosponsored this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents, none are Republicans, and Republicans hold the Senate majority with 55 of 100 seats, so the bill sits in a committee controlled by the opposing party.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would permanently bar drilling on the coastal plain, which the 2017 tax law had opened to oil and gas leasing. The industry loses access to a large untapped reserve; supporters of the bill argue that keeping it undeveloped is the public's gain.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and local communities dependent on resource development
industries.note: The state and its communities rely heavily on resource development revenue and jobs, and drilling supporters had counted the coastal plain as a source of both. Permanent wilderness status would end that potential revenue stream for good.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action in months, all 22 cosponsors from one party, and Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, the bill is very unlikely to advance on its own this Congress; its only realistic path is being folded into a larger must-pass bill after an election changes the Senate's balance.
